title: Infrastructure Australia Amendment (Cost Benefit Analysis and Other Measures) Bill 2014
short_title: Infrastructure Australia Amendment (Cost Benefit Analysis and Other Measures) Bill 2014

summary.attribution: Written by a model from the explanatory memorandum; not the record
sentences: This bill would clarify the role and administrative rules of Infrastructure Australia after a related Act starts.
It would require Infrastructure Australia to evaluate infrastructure proposals that involve at least $100 million in Commonwealth funding.
The $100 million threshold is set in 2014 dollars and would be indexed at least every five years.
changes: Clarifies the legislative and administrative arrangements for Infrastructure Australia.
Moves cost benefit analysis provisions to the correct part of the Infrastructure Australia Act 2008.
Adds a function requiring Infrastructure Australia to evaluate proposals with Commonwealth funding of at least $100 million.
summary.affected: Infrastructure Australia and entities proposing infrastructure projects that seek Commonwealth funding.

divisions.question: Anthony Albanese by leave—I move opposition amendments (2), (3), (6) and (7) together: (2) Schedule 1, item 2, page 3 (lines 11 to 13), omit "for investment in, or enhancements to, nationally significant infrastructure that involve Commonwealth funding", substitute "that involve capital expenditure". (3) Schedule 1, page 3 (after line 13), after item 2, insert: 2A At the end of section 5A Add: (5) The summary of a proposal evaluated during a quarter must also include: (a) either: (i) if the proposal involves capital expenditure of $100 million or more—a cost benefit analysis of the proposal prepared under section 5AA; or (ii) for any other proposal—a cost benefit analysis of the proposal if one has been prepared under that section; and (b) a summary of Infrastructure Australia's evaluation of the proposal. (6) Schedule 1, item 7, page 4 (after line 21), after subsection 39E(1), insert: (1A) The amount referred to in subparagraph 5A(5)(a)(i) is to be indexed at the same time, and by the same amount, as the amount referred to in subsection 5A(2). (7) Schedule 1, item 7, page 4 (line 22), omit "is", substitute "and subparagraph 5A(5)(a)(i) are". These amendments relate to Infrastructure Australia's evaluation of proposals. Amendment (2) relates to requiring a cost-benefit analysis of projects over $100 million. The government's wording gets the process back to front, and Labor's amendments will address that. Our amendments are consistent with the legislation adopted by the former Labor government relating to the Building Australia Fund and what Labor have moved for in recent months. It gives the $100 million commitment actual meaning. The effect of this specific amendment is twofold. Firstly, it gets the sequencing right around project proposals by correctly defining the trigger for a cost-benefit appraisal by Infrastructure Australia. Anthony Albanese by leave—I move opposition amendments (4) and (5): (4) Schedule 1, item 3, page 3 (line 21), omit "may", substitute "must". (5) Schedule 1, item 3, page 3 (line 26), omit "6", substitute "12". Item 4 requires Infrastructure Australia to approve a standard method for requiring assessments of proposals. This allows for costs and benefits of competing or alternative projects to be compared. This maintains the status quo in the existing act. The government's amendment makes standardisation optional for Infrastructure Australia. Labor's amendment will make a standard method a requirement, as is currently the case, and as is critical if we are examining where taxpayer dollars should go to which project where there are multiple bids for infrastructure projects. Given that there are many more bids for projects than will ever be funded, this is an important amendment. Amendment (5) is a minor amendment providing for better spacing of the first review of Infrastructure Australia's standard assessment method. This amendment requires the first review to occur by next September rather than March. I commend the amendments to the House. Warren Truss I commented earlier that the government had not had a chance to review the amendments. A superficial examination of this couple of amendments suggests that there may well be room for us to accept them, but I would want to study that beforehand. So, we will be opposing them, but there is a degree of superficial goodwill towards those two amendments. speeches.speaker: Anthony Albanese
speeches.brief: Argued that the Infrastructure Australia Amendment (Cost Benefit Analysis and Other Measures) Bill would let the government fund projects worth more than $100 million before any cost-benefit analysis, citing $3.5 billion already paid for the WestConnex and East West Link projects without full business cases, and moved amendments requiring analysis before funding is allocated.

speeches.speaker: Fiona Scott
speeches.brief: Argued in support of the Infrastructure Australia Amendment (Cost Benefit Analysis and Other Measures) Bill, saying it would require Infrastructure Australia to conduct cost-benefit analysis before projects worth $100 million or more are added to priority lists, and said the WestConnex project would deliver more than $20 billion in economic benefits and create 10000 jobs by 2023.

speeches.speaker: Fiona Scott
speeches.brief: Supported the Infrastructure Australia Amendment bill, explaining it would give Infrastructure Australia a greater role in rigorously assessing project cost-benefit analysis while leaving final infrastructure funding decisions with the minister.

speeches.speaker: Andrew Giles
speeches.brief: Criticized the Infrastructure Australia Amendment bill for applying cost-benefit analysis only to projects where Commonwealth funding exceeds $100 million rather than total project value, and cited an Infrastructure Australia analysis showing Melbourne's East West Link has a cost-benefit ratio of just 0.5 to 0.8 despite the government committing $1.5 billion, including $1 billion for an unplanned second stage.

speeches.speaker: David Coleman
speeches.brief: Supported the Infrastructure Australia Amendment bill, contrasting it with Labor's NBN cost blowout from an original $10 billion estimate to about $70 billion while only $6.5 billion delivered coverage to three per cent of the population, and highlighted the federal government's $1.5 billion cash contribution and $2 billion concessional loan for the WestConnex M5 East duplication.

speeches.speaker: Alannah MacTiernan
speeches.brief: Criticized the Perth Freight Link's $740 million Roe Highway extension and $460 million in additional works as hastily assembled without proper cost-benefit analysis, and disputed the assistant minister's infrastructure funding figures, showing Western Australia receives just 10.37 per cent of the $45.3 billion infrastructure budget despite producing over 16 per cent of Australia's GDP.

speeches.speaker: Melissa Price
speeches.brief: Supported the Infrastructure Australia Amendment bill and the government's $50 billion infrastructure investment program, citing local commitments in her electorate of Durack including $174 million for the North West Coastal Highway, $74.7 million for the Great Northern Highway between Waddington and Walebing, and a completed $260 million upgrade at Port Hedland.

speeches.speaker: Pat Conroy
speeches.brief: Argued the East West Link's cost-benefit ratio of just 0.8, meaning $1 spent returns only 80 cents, contrasts with the $1.7 billion Hunter Expressway's ratio of about five, and recalled Howard-era regional rorts including $5.7 million for a heritage railway that went bust twice and derailed, to warn against funding projects before proper cost-benefit analysis.

speeches.speaker: Angus Taylor
speeches.brief: Supported the bill, citing an infrastructure backlog estimated at $455 billion to $770 billion, noted only 14 per cent of Labor's $80 billion stimulus spending went to productive infrastructure with none approved by Infrastructure Australia, and outlined the government's $50 billion transport infrastructure commitment alongside a $5 billion Asset Recycling Fund to encourage states to sell and reinvest in assets.

speeches.speaker: Terri Butler
speeches.brief: Criticized the government for failing to require cost-benefit analysis on the Asset Recycling Fund, which Labor unsuccessfully tried to amend, and accused it of breaking pre-election promises with $80 billion in health and education cuts, a 20 per cent cut to university funding and fee deregulation that could create $100,000 degrees at the University of Western Australia.

speeches.speaker: Karen McNamara
speeches.brief: Supported the Infrastructure Australia bill, citing a cost-benefit analysis showing the coalition's mixed-technology NBN approach delivers $18 billion more net benefit than Labor's plan, which would have cost an extra $29 billion and taken four years longer, and detailed local investment in her electorate of Dobell including the NorthConnex tunnel, expected to cut travel time by up to 15 minutes.

speeches.speaker: Matt Thistlethwaite
speeches.brief: Criticized the government for handing $2 billion to New South Wales for WestConnex and $1.5 billion to Victoria for the East West Link without any cost-benefit analysis, noting WestConnex fails to connect to Port Botany, Australia's busiest container port, and cited a Sydney Morning Herald report finding coalition electorates were favoured three to one in infrastructure funding.

speeches.speaker: Ken O'Dowd
speeches.brief: Supported the Infrastructure Australia bill, citing the government's $50 billion infrastructure program expected to leverage more than $125 billion in investment, $16.4 billion more than Labor promised, and described the Dawson Highway in his electorate of Flynn, where five bridges in 120 kilometres have load limits preventing B-double cattle transport.

speeches.speaker: Lisa Chesters
speeches.brief: Supported the Infrastructure Australia bill, contrasting Victoria's $8 billion East West Link, which received $1.5 billion in federal funding without a published business case, with the Regional Rail Link, a $4.4 billion Labor-funded project, the largest Commonwealth urban public transport investment in Australian history, which created 4,000 construction jobs and will add 23 extra peak Metro services.

speeches.speaker: Paul Fletcher
speeches.brief: Cited the Vertigan panel's cost-benefit analysis of the NBN, finding superfast broadband would deliver more than $40 billion in total benefits and that the government's multi-technology mix approach offers $18 billion in net benefits, $16 billion more than Labor's fibre-to-the-premises plan, which the analysis found would have delivered only about $2 billion in net benefits.

speeches.speaker: Kelvin Thomson
speeches.brief: Opposed the East West Link, citing former Infrastructure Australia head Michael Deegan's disclosure of an unpublished cost-benefit ratio of just 0.8, meaning 80 cents return for every dollar spent, and a University College London study finding motorists would need to be charged a minimum $10.50 a trip for investors to profit, while CityLink founder Alan Hale called the project the wrong priority.

speeches.speaker: Teresa Gambaro
speeches.brief: Supported the bill, arguing that it would clarify Infrastructure Australia's arrangements, require evaluation of nationally significant proposals involving Commonwealth funding of at least $100 million, and improve transparency and accountability in infrastructure spending. Emphasised the importance of cost-benefit analysis, coordinated planning and reliable infrastructure, citing the government's $50 billion Infrastructure Investment program and Queensland's infrastructure needs.

speeches.speaker: Nola Marino
speeches.brief: Supported the bill, arguing that cost-benefit analysis was needed for nationally significant infrastructure and proposals involving Commonwealth funding of at least $100 million. Highlighted transport pressures and infrastructure priorities in Western Australia's South West, including the Bunbury Outer Ring Road, freight rail capacity and a regional airport in Busselton, while describing the bill's approach to investment assessment as sound.

speeches.speaker: Craig Kelly
speeches.brief: Supported the bill, arguing that cost-benefit analysis should account for all project costs and benefits. Criticised the Moorebank intermodal project's analysis for excluding land, road, bridge, congestion, hospital access and particulate-emission costs, and for overstating demand, concluding that private proponents should pay the true economic cost and contribute to required upgrades.

speeches.speaker: Luke Simpkins
speeches.brief: Supported the bill, arguing that infrastructure funding must be assessed for efficiency, productivity and public benefit. Cited the $50 billion infrastructure commitment and projects including NorthLinkWA, while describing Infrastructure Australia's proposed assessments, audit, 15-year plan and transparency arrangements and identifying possible road and overpass projects in Cowan.

speeches.speaker: Ed Husic
speeches.brief: Asked how much money the government had committed to infrastructure during its first year and why it was only then seeking cost-benefit analysis through the bill.

speeches.speaker: Laurie Ferguson
speeches.brief: Reported that the Human Rights Committee examined 12 bills, found nine required no further scrutiny, deferred one and identified two for further examination; it concluded that 10 of 12 matters concerning the Social Services and Other Legislation Amendment (2014 Budget Measures No. 2) Bill 2014 were compatible with human rights.

speeches.speaker: David Gillespie
speeches.brief: Supported the Infrastructure Australia Amendment (Cost Benefit Analysis and Other Measures) Bill, arguing for independent governance, cost-benefit analysis of nationally significant projects involving Commonwealth funding of at least $100 million, and a 15-year infrastructure plan; cited the Pacific Highway and Bucketts Highway works.
